1.9 Information Economics

Asymmetric information

Section titled “Asymmetric information”

So far we have assumed that buyers and sellers both know the quality of what is traded. In reality one side often knows more: the owner of a used car knows what has gone wrong with it, a person buying insurance knows their own health, and a company’s manager knows whether they have worked hard. When one side of a transaction knows something the other side does not, there is asymmetric information.

Asymmetric information comes in two kinds:

  • Hidden information: before the transaction, one side does not know the other side’s type, for example whether a car is good or bad, or whether a policyholder is high or low risk. It leads to adverse selection.
  • Hidden action: after the transaction, one side cannot see what the other side does, for example whether a policyholder is careful or whether a manager works hard. It leads to moral hazard.

Adverse selection

Section titled “Adverse selection”

A used-car market has two kinds of car: good cars and bad cars (in American slang, “lemons”). Buyers cannot tell which kind a car is; owners can.

Kind of carValue to buyers (dollars)Owner’s lowest price (dollars)
Good car10,0008,000
Lemon4,0003,000

For each kind of car, buyers value it more than its owner does, so if quality were public, every car should be sold: that makes total surplus as large as possible (consumer surplus).

Now suppose half of the cars for sale are good. Buyers are risk neutral and pay at most the average value (expected value):

0.5×10,000+0.5×4,000=7,0000.5 \times 10{,}000 + 0.5 \times 4{,}000 = 7{,}0000.5×10,000+0.5×4,000=7,000

This price is below the 8,000 that owners of good cars require, so they do not sell. Buyers can work this out too: only owners of lemons are willing to sell at 7,000, so buyers will pay only 4,000. In the end only lemons are traded; good cars, although they are worth more to buyers, do not sell at all.

When the less-informed side ends up facing exactly the counterparties that are worst for it, this is called adverse selection. This model is called the market for lemons, proposed by George Akerlof in 1970. How high must the share of good cars be for their owners to stay in the market? Use the figure below to find out.

Check C1
In Figure 2-1, raise the share of good cars step by step and find roughly the share at which owners of good cars start to be willing to stay in the market; then compute it exactly. If 70% of the cars for sale are good, what is the most buyers will pay, and which cars are traded?

Insurance markets also have adverse selection. An insurer that cannot tell high risks from low risks can only set the premium by the average risk; for low-risk people this premium is too high, so they do not buy, the remaining buyers are riskier on average, the premium must rise again, and things can keep getting worse. The same happens in financial markets:

  • Issuing new shares: managers know better than investors what the company is worth. Issuing new shares pays best when the share price is above what the managers think it is worth, so investors read a share issue as a sign that the price is too high, and share prices often fall when companies announce an issue.
  • Lending: when a bank raises its interest rate, the borrowers willing to accept the higher rate tend to be riskier. So banks often limit the amount they lend and require collateral instead of simply raising the rate.
Check C2
Half of the potential buyers of a health insurance policy are low-risk people with expected claims of 200 dollars a year; half are high-risk people with expected claims of 800 dollars. Because they are risk averse, low-risk people would pay a premium of at most 300 dollars, and high-risk people at most 1,000 dollars. The insurer cannot tell the two groups apart, must charge all buyers the same premium, and sets it equal to the average expected claim of the buyers (breaking even).
(a) If both groups buy, what is the premium? Will low-risk people buy?
(b) In the end, who buys insurance, and at what premium? Why is this outcome inefficient?

Signaling and screening

Section titled “Signaling and screening”

Can the owner of a good car prove that the car is good? Just saying “my car is good” does not help, because owners of lemons say the same. What is needed is an action that is cheap for owners of good cars and expensive for owners of lemons, such as a one-year warranty: a good car seldom needs repairs, so the warranty costs almost nothing; a lemon often breaks down, so the warranty is very costly. When the better-informed side reveals its type through such a costly action, this is called signaling. What conditions does a signal need in order to work? Derive them in Exercises Question 3.

Other examples:

  • Education: even if a degree did not make people more productive, able people find it easier to complete one, so a degree can signal ability to employers (Michael Spence).
  • Paying steady dividends for many years: a company with unsteady cash flow would find it hard to keep this up.
  • Company founders and managers buying a large amount of their own company’s shares with their own money.

Conversely, the less-informed side can design a set of choices so that the other side reveals its type by what it chooses. This is called screening. An insurer offers two policies at the same time: a low premium with a high deductible, or a high premium with full coverage. Low-risk people seldom make claims and prefer the high deductible; high-risk people choose full coverage. A bank that requires collateral or a down payment is also screening: only borrowers confident in their own projects are willing to put their own assets at stake.

Check C3
Use the lesson's used-car market (a good car is worth 10,000 to buyers and its owner's lowest price is 8,000; a lemon is worth 4,000 to buyers). Sellers can offer a one-year warranty. Expected repair costs within a year: 200 dollars for a good car and 7,000 dollars for a lemon. If buyers believe that only good cars come with a warranty, they will pay 10,000 for a car with a warranty; a car without one is treated as a lemon and is worth only 4,000.
(a) Will owners of good cars offer the warranty? Will owners of lemons copy them? Does the warranty separate the two kinds of car?
(b) What happens if a lemon's expected repair cost for a year is only 5,000 dollars?

Moral hazard

Section titled “Moral hazard”

After a contract is signed, one side may take actions the other side cannot see, and these actions affect the other side’s losses. Someone with full car insurance may drive less carefully than before, because the insurer bears the loss. When a contract relieves one side of the full consequences of its actions and thereby changes those actions, this is called moral hazard.

The remedy is to make the acting side bear part of the consequences: deductibles, sharing a proportion of each loss (coinsurance), premium discounts for safe driving, or closer monitoring.

Moral hazard is common in finance:

  • If large banks expect the government to rescue them when they get into trouble (“too big to fail”), the gains from taking risk are theirs while part of the losses fall on taxpayers, so they take more risk. This adds to the problem of externality.
  • Deposit insurance prevents runs, but it also means depositors no longer care whether their bank is sound, so banks face less discipline. That is why places with deposit insurance usually also regulate bank capital.
Check C4
A renter can spend 50 dollars on fire-safety equipment and be more careful. If the renter does, the probability of a 1,000-dollar loss within a year is 10%; if not, it is 20%.
(a) Without insurance, will the renter take care?
(b) What about with full insurance?
(c) The insurer sets a deductible DDD (the renter bears the first DDD dollars of each loss). How large must DDD be at least for the renter to take care? (Ignore risk aversion.)

The principal-agent problem

Section titled “The principal-agent problem”

Many economic relationships involve one party asking another to act on its behalf: shareholders hire managers to run the company, investors hire fund managers to manage their money, and clients hire advisers for advice. The party who hires is called the principal, and the party who acts is called the agent. When the agent’s interests are not fully aligned with the principal’s and the principal cannot fully observe what the agent does or how well, this is called the principal-agent problem. It is a form of moral hazard and is especially important in investing:

  • Shareholders and managers: managers may pursue the size of the company rather than its profit (a larger company brings more status and higher pay), enjoy too many perks, or sacrifice long-term value for short-term results.
  • Investors and fund managers: if a fund charges fees based on the assets it manages, the manager’s income depends mainly on size rather than performance. The manager then has a reason to focus on attracting money, or to hold almost the same positions as the index (so as not to fall behind it and lose money) while charging fees for active management. If the manager shares the gains but not the losses, the manager has a reason to take too much risk (see Exercises Question 2).
  • Clients and advisers: if an adviser’s income comes from sales commissions on products, the adviser has a reason to recommend high-commission products, which often also have high fees.

There are three kinds of remedy for the principal-agent problem:

  • Incentives: tie the agent’s pay to the principal’s interests, for example by having managers own the company’s shares or paying bonuses based on long-term results. But tying pay to results also passes the risk of the results to the agent; agents are usually risk averse (risk aversion) and demand higher pay in return. So pay usually does not depend entirely on results. How the agent’s share affects the agent’s effort and the principal’s payoff is examined in Exercises Question 4.
  • Monitoring: boards of directors, audits, disclosure.
  • Legal duties: in the United States, registered investment advisers owe their clients a fiduciary duty under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and must put the clients’ interests first; since 2020, broker-dealers must follow the Securities and Exchange Commission’s (SEC) Regulation Best Interest.

For an investor, the most practical step is to ask: where does the income of the person managing your money or advising you come from? Stage 6 uses this question again and again when choosing funds and advisers.

Check C5
A financial adviser charges clients nothing; all of the adviser's income comes from sales commissions paid by the funds the adviser recommends.
(a) Who is the principal and who is the agent? Where do their interests differ?
(b) Why is it hard for the principal to detect the problem?
(c) Give two ways to reduce the problem.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Asymmetric information: one side of a transaction knows more. Hidden information before the transaction leads to adverse selection; hidden action after it leads to moral hazard.
  • Adverse selection: pricing by average quality drives the good types out of the market, and at worst only the worst type remains (the market for lemons). Insurance, share issues and lending all show adverse selection.
  • Signaling: the better-informed side reveals its type through a costly action. Screening: the less-informed side designs choices that make the other side reveal its type.
  • Moral hazard: a contract relieves one side of the full consequences of its actions. Deductibles, shared losses and monitoring reduce it.
  • The principal-agent problem: the agent’s interests differ from the principal’s, and the agent’s actions are hard to observe. The remedies are incentives, monitoring and legal duties; the stronger the incentive, the more risk the agent bears.

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
In a used-car market, car quality vvv is uniformly distributed between 0 and 10,000 dollars (vvv is the owner's value of the car), and buyers value a car of quality vvv at 1.5v1.5v1.5v. Only owners know vvv; buyers are risk neutral and know only the average quality of the cars for sale.
(a) If the market price is ppp, which owners are willing to sell? What is the average quality of the cars for sale? How much are buyers willing to pay?
(b) Show that no price except p=0p = 0p=0 makes what buyers are willing to pay equal to ppp. What does this show?
Question 2
A fund manager is paid 20% of the fund's return for the year, but nothing if the return is negative (the manager bears no losses). There are two strategies: a safe one with a certain return of 5% a year, and an aggressive one with a return of +40% or −30% each year with equal probability.
(a) What is the expected return of each strategy? If investors are risk averse, which do they prefer?
(b) What is the manager's expected pay under each strategy (as a percentage of fund assets)? Which strategy will the manager choose?
(c) What is the problem with this pay structure? Suggest one improvement.

Question 5
A commission-paid adviser recommends that a client put 100,000 dollars into fund X, which charges a 5% sales commission on purchase (paid to the adviser) and then an expense ratio of 1.0% a year. The alternative is index fund Y, with no sales commission and an expense ratio of 0.05% a year. Both funds earn 7% a year before fees, and fees are taken directly out of the yearly return. The money is held for 20 years.
(a) What is the value of each choice after 20 years? How large is the difference?
(b) How much does the adviser get from this recommendation? Use the principal-agent idea to explain why this arrangement costs the client.
